meta.title: Adobe, Giving It Away
meta.dek: Adobe has stopped raising prices and started giving its creative tools away to win the next generation of users, and it has handed the company to the man who built its smaller business. At $256 the stock prices in almost no growth. Is that a bargain, or is the market right about the creative seat?
meta.price_note: Oct 21, 2026, 1:04 PM EDT (intraday; StockAnalysis $255.97 at 1:00 PM)
meta.type: Software — subscription creative, document and customer-experience platform

verdict.sentence: Adobe still beats its own guidance, but it has paused price increases and is giving its creative tools away to defend the seat against AI; at $256 the probability-weighted case pays [[pw_return]] a year, close to half of it from the buyback, and clears 13% only at [[entry]].
verdict.breaks_if: the FY2027 ARR guide on December 9, the new CEO's first, implies organic growth below ~8%. The buyback can carry per-share earnings for a while, but not for a book of business slowing toward GDP growth.
verdict.next: MAX Nov 10–12; Q4 + FY27 targets Dec 9

call: At $256 the market is pricing Adobe's creative business as a melting asset. The price implies Bear odds of [[implied_bear]] at a 9% discount rate, almost exactly the 35% I assign, and it needs owner earnings per share to grow only about [[Priced-in.cagr]] a year, mostly from the buyback. The market isn't wrong. Organic ARR growth is slowing toward 8%. Q3 net new ARR of $0.40B was down roughly 37% from a year earlier. And the Creative Cloud price increases that carried 2024–25 were deferred in June so that a freemium funnel could run, with no conversion rate disclosed. The CEO-designate built the customer-experience business, not the creative one. What keeps the case alive is cash: about $8.5B of owner earnings a year, nearly all of it spent retiring ~7% of the shares. That turns ~6% revenue growth into [[compounding]] compounding at a flat multiple. It is a good return, but not 13%. The verb is not probability-fragile: break-even Bear odds are [[breakeven_bear]] against 35% assigned. The price that clears the hurdle is [[entry]], where the stock traded as recently as June.

tests.test: the FY2027 total ARR growth target (Dec 9) at or above 9% excluding acquisitions, and a disclosed free-to-paid conversion rate or paid Firefly subscriber count by the Q1 FY2027 print (mid-March 2027).
tests.if_fail: move 10 points from Base to Bear (PW EV [[test1.pw_ev]], [[test1.pw_return]]/yr) → stays **[[test1.verb]]**, entry falls to [[test1.entry]]; with no conversion data by March, the Bull is cut to 10% as well.

tests.claim: That the creative franchise holds through a CEO change centred on customer experience.
tests.test: reported Creative & Marketing Professionals subscription growth of at least 11% in Q4 FY2026 (Dec 9) and Q1 FY2027 (March), against 13% in Q3, about 3 points of which is SEMrush until April 2027, with no further senior creative-product departures.
tests.if_fail: Base Creative revenue held flat for five years (Base value $428; PW EV [[test2.pw_ev]], [[test2.pw_return]]/yr) → stays **[[test2.verb]]**, entry [[test2.entry]]; moat trend recorded as narrowing faster.

tests.claim: That AI costs don't take the margin.
tests.test: the FY2027 non-GAAP operating-margin target (Dec 9) at or above 42%, against ~45% for FY2026 and ~44% guided for Q4.
tests.if_fail: Base terminal margin cut ~3 points to ~41% (Base value $421; PW EV [[test3.pw_ev]], [[test3.pw_return]]/yr) → stays **[[test3.verb]]**, entry [[test3.entry]]; per-share growth then rests almost wholly on the buyback.

model_build.note: Base case. FY2026 is calibrated to the $24.45–24.50 non-GAAP EPS target; the split of revenue and margin into three businesses is the author's estimate, since Adobe reports subscription revenue by customer group and gross profit by legacy segment but no segment operating income. Margins move linearly from FY2026 to the FY2031 input. Owner earnings deduct after-tax SBC, which non-GAAP EPS excludes. Source: author's model (model.json).

scenarios.note: Values are FY2031 owner earnings per share × the exit multiple; annual return is the price change to that value (no dividend). Probabilities apply to Bull, Base and Bear. The Priced-in row is solved along Bear→Base and the Hurdle row along Base→Bull, both at a 14× owner-earnings exit. Source: author's model.

return_math.optionality: None valued separately. Freemium conversion and resumed pricing are the Bull; Topaz Labs (~$340M) is too small to move the value.
return_math.epv: About $176 per share on five-year average owner earnings ($6.2B ÷ 9%, 391M shares), or ≈$239 on trailing owner earnings of $8.5B after ~$1.1B of net debt. On current earnings, only ~7% of the price pays for growth. The Bear ($179) sits below trailing EPV because it names the damage: creative revenue shrinking 3% a year and margin down ~6 points. EPV ÷ invested capital ≈ 7, so the business is still a franchise.
return_math.base_rate: The Bull needs ~8.7% nominal (~6% real) revenue growth for five years from $26.6B. Of companies above $25B, 31.8% reach ≥5% real growth and 13.7% reach ≥10%, so the Bull is plausible. The Base's ~5.8% nominal sits near the middle of the class (probable); the Bear is probable for a franchise under technology attack.
return_math.year_ten: Documents and customer experience should still grow high single digits at year ten; Creative is the open question. At 14× owner earnings (1.7% implied perpetual growth), the terminal multiple isn't doing the work; the buyback is.
return_math.rr_note: . The figure is large because the multiple is already low, not because the Bull is likely.
return_math.note: Computed rows come from model.json; EPV, base rate and year ten are the author's. 10-year Treasury from [Treasury.gov daily par yields](https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve&field_tdr_date_value=2026), Oct 20, 2026.
return_math.price_implied: At 9%, spot needs [[Priced-in.owner_eps]] of owner earnings per share in FY2031 ([[Priced-in.cagr]] a year) at 14×: revenue up ~4% a year, margin ~42%, ~4% net buyback. Perpetual cross-check: trailing owner earnings of $8.5B are 8.5% of the ~$101B enterprise value, so g ≈ 9% − 8.5% ≈ 0.5%.
